about: Energy references for the Rex lab energy ladder (BRIEF-gui.md section 6), researched 13 Oct 2026: seven topics (an audit of the old rungs, then six energy bands), each researched, then checked by a skeptic who fetched every source, then compiled with the corrections applied. Merged by hand; see research/reviews/gui-c-research.json for the topics, the skeptics' checks and the merge decisions.

facts.label: Lifting a 100 g apple one metre (energy it gains)
facts.display: about 1 J (0.101 kg × 9.81 m/s² × 1 m)

sources.title: USDA FoodData Central, SR Legacy FDC 171688 'Apples, raw, with skin' (NDB 09003): portion weights, JSON behind the FDC food page
NIST CODATA: standard acceleration of gravity, 9.806 65 m/s² (exact)

facts.notes: E = m g h with m = 0.101 kg (energy_apple_extra_small_mass, USDA 'extra small (2-1/2" dia)'), g = 9.80665 m/s^2 exact (earth_standard_gravity), h = 1 m: 0.9905 J. The energy the apple gains, not the food energy the lifter burns (muscles turn most of that into heat). A common illustration of one joule (not sourced here). Local gravity differs from standard by under 0.5%. Page says '100 g apple', not 'small apple', because USDA's 'small' is 149 g. Skeptic: recomputed 0.990 J and proposed this as the bottom rung so energies near 1 J stay on the ladder (ladder.js: below 0.86 J is beyond it).

facts.label: Composition B: strength relative to TNT, by test
facts.display: 1.10-1.16x TNT in air blast; 1.30-1.33x in the Trauzl, plate-dent and ballistic-mortar tests

sources.title: US Army Materiel Command AMCP 706-177 (1971), Composition B data sheet, pp. 46 and 48 (PDF pp. 54 and 56)

facts.notes: Read from the page images. p. 46: 'Ballistic Mortar, % TNT: 133'; 'Trauzl Test, % TNT: 130'; 'Plate Dent ... Brisance, % TNT 132'. p. 48, 'Blast (Relative to TNT)': 'Air: Peak Pressure 110, Impulse 110, Energy 116; Air, Confined: Impulse 75; Under Water: Peak Pressure 110, Impulse 108, Energy 121; Underground: 104, 97, crater radius cubed 107'. Relative strength depends on the test. Value 1.16 is the air-blast energy ratio; range 1.10 (air peak pressure and impulse) to 1.33 (ballistic mortar). Replaces the earlier 'claimed' 1.33 from a Wikipedia table tagged 'citation needed': the Army handbook is a primary source for 1.33, by ballistic mortar. Not needed for the grenade rung, which uses the heat of detonation. Skeptic: 'does not support 1.33' deleted; range widened to 1.10-1.33; value 1.16.

facts.display: 12 ft-lb (16.3 J) at the muzzle; above this an air rifle needs a firearm certificate in England and Wales (air pistols: 6 ft-lb, 8.1 J). Northern Ireland's line is 1 J

sources.title: The Firearms (Dangerous Air Weapons) Rules 1969, SI 1969/47, rule 2(1) (legislation.gov.uk, as made)
Home Office, Guide on Firearms Licensing Law (accessible version, last updated 18 Sep 2026), para 2.46
Firearms (Northern Ireland) Order 2004, Schedule 1 Part 9 (legislation.gov.uk)

Skeptic: key, label and page phrase changed from 'UK', because Northern Ireland (Firearms (NI) Order 2004, Sch 1 Pt 9 para 9(2)) licenses air guns above 1 J; Home Office guide added to show the 12 ft-lb line is current. facts.label: Usain Bolt: body mass (as listed)
facts.display: 95 kg (height 1.96 m), as listed in a 2019 biomechanics paper

sources.title: Coh M. 2019, Usain Bolt: biomechanical model of sprint technique, Facta Universitatis PES 17(1):1-13 (PDF)
Coh et al. 2018, The kinematics of Usain Bolt's maximal sprint velocity, Kinesiology 50(2):172-180 (abstract page)

facts.notes: Coh 2019: 'Usain Bolt (age: 25, height: 1.96 m, weight: 95 kg, BMI: 24.7)'. A listed figure, not a race-day weighing. Coh et al. 2018 abstract: 'vertical ground reaction force equal to 4.2 times body weight (3932 N)', implying 3932 / (4.2 x 9.80665) = 95.5 kg; consistent, but the same research group, so not independent. facts.label: Hubble Space Telescope: orbital speed
facts.display: about 17,000 mph (27,300 km/h, 7.6 km/s) at 340 miles (547 km) up

sources.title: NASA Science: A NASA Refresher on Hubble Facts for the 25th Anniversary (Goddard, 16 Apr 2015)
NASA Facts: Hubble Space Telescope - An Overview (fact sheet PDF)

facts.notes: NASA refresher: 'Altitude of 340 miles (295 nautical miles, 547 km ... Time to Complete One Orbit: ~95 minutes Speed: ~17,000 mph (27,300 kph)'. Fact sheet: 'the speed of about 5 miles (8 km) per second' (rounder). 17,000 mph = 7,600 m/s; 27,300 km/h = 7,583 m/s. Check: circular-orbit speed sqrt(GM/r) at 547 km (GM = 3.986e14 m^3/s^2, R = 6,371 km) is 7,591 m/s. Speed relative to Earth's centre. Input to energy_hubble_orbit_kinetic, not a rung. Skeptic: confirmed; 547 km is the 2015 height, and Hubble has since sunk somewhat lower (skeptic's figure, not sourced), which raises the speed by under 0.3%.

facts.label: International Space Station: orbital speed
facts.display: about 7.7 km/s (from NASA's 90-minute orbit); NASA rounds it to 'five miles per second' (8.0 km/s); about 7.66 km/s at its real height

sources.title: NASA: Space Station Facts and Figures

facts.notes: NASA: crew 'traveling at a speed of five miles per second, orbiting Earth about every 90 minutes'; 'In 24 hours, the space station makes 16 orbits of Earth'. Circular orbit: v = (2 pi GM / T)^(1/3) with T = 5,400 s and GM = 3.986e14 m^3/s^2 gives 7,741 m/s. high_si: NASA's rounder 'five miles per second' (8,047 m/s). low_si: circular speed at about 420 km, 7,660 m/s (physics; the height is not sourced). Skeptic: the 90-minute period is rounded and implies an orbit only about 280 km up, so 7,741 m/s is about 1% high; low_si added. Speed relative to Earth's centre. Input to energy_iss_orbit_kinetic, not a rung.
